pages.x: Charles I believed kings were chosen by God and answered to no one else. He ruled for eleven years without Parliament, raised taxes it had not agreed, and angered Puritans with his church reforms. When Scotland rose in 1639 he had to call Parliament back, and it wanted power.

In January 1642 Charles marched into the House of Commons with soldiers to arrest five of his fiercest critics. They had slipped away, and the Speaker would not say where. Charles left London, and in August raised his royal standard at Nottingham.

The king's men, many of them gentry with long hair, were called Cavaliers. Parliament's, many of them Puritans with short-cropped hair, were Roundheads. Families were split, and towns changed hands again and again.

Oliver Cromwell, a Puritan squire with no training as a soldier, built a disciplined cavalry, the Ironsides, and helped create Parliament's New Model Army. At Naseby in 1645 it destroyed the king's main army.
Fighting, and the disease that came with the armies, killed perhaps 200,000 people in England and Wales, a larger share of the people than the First World War. In Ireland the toll was far worse.

Charles was tried for treason against his own people in January 1649 and refused to recognise the court. On 30 January he was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. He wore two shirts so that he would not shiver in the cold and seem afraid.

England became a republic, the Commonwealth. Cromwell crushed Ireland, with massacres at Drogheda and Wexford in 1649, and in 1653 made himself Lord Protector. Theatres were shut and Christmas celebrations banned.

Beaten at Worcester in 1651, the young Charles II hid in an oak tree while soldiers searched the woods below, then escaped to France in disguise. Hundreds of English pubs are still called the Royal Oak.

Cromwell died in 1658, and without him the republic fell apart. In 1660 Parliament invited Charles II home. Cromwell's body was dug up, hanged and beheaded, and his head stood on a pole outside Westminster Hall for years.

The monarchy came back, but kings could never again rule without Parliament. The ideas argued in the war, about rights, government by consent and even votes for all men, travelled to America and beyond.
